question: What is the primary goal of injection safety in clinical practice?

options.A: To speed up the administration of intravenous medications
options.B: To prevent harm to patients, health workers, and the community
options.C: To eliminate the need for wearing gloves during procedures
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing medical syringes

explanation: Injection safety encompasses measures that protect the patient receiving the injection, the nurse administering it, and the surrounding community from hazardous waste. [learn more](GNS122_U4_T1#GNS122_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why is proper injection safety so important for nurses?

options.A: Injections are rare procedures that need special certification
options.B: Injections are done daily and can spread serious infections if mishandled
options.C: Hospital management uses injection logs to grade nursing speed
options.D: Patients expect disposable equipment for financial reasons

explanation: You'll give lots of injections! Because they happen so often, even a tiny slip in safety can quickly pass an infection to many people. Staying sharp keeps everyone safe.

question: Which of these best describes an unsafe injection practice?

options.A: Giving an intramuscular shot without asking the patient's age first
options.B: Any injection action that puts patients or staff at risk of preventable harm
options.C: Using a plastic syringe instead of a glass one
options.D: Giving an injection past normal visiting hours

explanation: If it puts anyone at risk of harm through contamination, reuse, or bad handling, it's unsafe. Trust your gut—if it feels risky, it probably is!

question: Which of these is a clear example of an unsafe injection habit?

options.A: Using a contaminated needle to enter a single-dose medication vial
options.B: Using a fresh, sterile needle and syringe for every single patient
options.C: Dropping a used syringe straight into a safety box
options.D: Cleaning the skin with an alcohol swab before the poke

explanation: Never use a needle that has touched a surface or a patient to draw more medicine. It contaminates the whole vial and puts the next person in danger.

question: Which of these is NOT a safe way to handle used needles?

options.A: Putting sharps containers right next to where you work
options.B: Avoiding bending needles before throwing them away
options.C: Dropping the whole syringe and needle into a safety box
options.D: Recapping needles using both hands right after use

explanation: Using both hands to recap is a top way nurses accidentally stick themselves. Always avoid it!

question: You need to give medications to two patients in your ward. What should you do with your equipment?

options.A: Rinse the syringe with hot water between patients
options.B: Change only the needle and keep the same syringe barrel
options.C: Use the same syringe if the drug is prescribed for both
options.D: Use a fresh, sterile syringe and needle for each patient

explanation: Syringes and needles are strictly single-use. Never share them between patients—ever!

question: What is a major reason why unsafe injections happen in low-resource clinics?

options.A: Having too many nurses on duty at night
options.B: Having way too many sterile water supplies
options.C: Shortages of disposable syringes and safety boxes
options.D: Too many mandatory infection control classes

explanation: When basic supplies run low, healthcare workers are put in tough spots. Advocating for proper supplies is a big part of nursing advocacy.

question: How can a severe shortage of nurses lead to unsafe injections?

options.A: It gives nurses extra time to clean equipment
options.B: It automatically gets rid of multi-dose vials
options.C: It causes rushed procedures where safety steps get skipped
options.D: It forces patients to inject themselves

explanation: When you're overworked and tired, it's easy to rush. Staying aware helps us protect our patients even on busy shifts.

question: Which infections are most commonly spread through unsafe injections?

options.A: Respiratory viruses like the common cold
options.C: Blood-borne viruses like Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV

explanation: Injections go straight past the skin barrier into tissues and blood vessels, making it easy for blood-borne viruses to travel if gear isn't sterile.

question: Why are accidental needlestick injuries so scary for healthcare workers?

options.A: They stop the worker from ever touching medical tools again
options.C: They instantly trigger severe allergies to latex
options.D: They can push infected blood straight into the nurse's bloodstream

explanation: A hollow needle often carries leftover blood from a patient. That's why safe disposal isn't just about the patient—it protects YOU too!

question: What is a major cause of unsafe injection risks in informal healthcare settings?

options.B: Too much government checking of pharmacies
options.D: Not enough clean, single-use equipment available

explanation: When places lack a steady supply of cheap, disposable syringes, dangerous reuse habits can creep in. Community health education helps fix this!

question: Why is teaching community members about injection safety so important in Nigeria?

options.A: To cut down the cost of running clinics
options.C: To help patients understand they don't always need an injection
options.D: To teach patients to give themselves IV drugs at home

explanation: Many people believe injections work faster than tablets, leading to a huge demand for unnecessary shots. Educating the public keeps everyone safer.

question: Where is the best place to keep your sharps disposal box during an injection?

options.A: In the nurse's station for later
options.B: Locked in a store room down the hall
options.C: On the floor right under the patient's bed
options.D: Right within arm's reach of your workspace

explanation: Keep your safety box close! Walking around with an open, used needle just asks for an accidental poke.

question: What is the big advantage of using single-dose medication vials?

options.A: They let nurses reuse syringes safely
options.B: They make the medicine taste sweeter
options.C: They completely stop the risk of contaminating shared medicine bottles
options.D: They mean fewer patients will need shots

explanation: Single-dose vials are used once and thrown away. No sharing means no chance of passing germs into the next dose!

question: What is a key professional duty of every nurse when it comes to injection safety?

options.A: Hiding unsafe practices to protect the hospital's image
options.B: Refusing unsafe practices and speaking up for proper supplies
options.C: Reusing needles when the hospital budget is tight
options.D: Leaving all injections to untrained volunteers

explanation: As a nurse, your primary loyalty is to safety. You have an ethical duty to speak up against dangerous shortcuts and shortages.

question: You see a senior nurse recapping a needle with both hands. What is the best way to handle this?

options.A: Kindly remind them of the risk and suggest a safer way
options.B: Report them to the police right away
options.C: Ignore it because they have more experience
options.D: Copy them so you can finish your work faster

explanation: Be polite and respectful, but speak up! Friendly peer reminders build a safer, more supportive workplace for everyone.
